headline: UN lets Western Sahara mission lapse
summary: The UN Security Council failed to renew MINURSO after a Russian veto of a US draft and a failed Russian counter-draft, so the Western Sahara mission's mandate ends on 31 October.
display_body: The UN Security Council on Friday 30 October failed to renew the UN peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara (MINURSO), so its 35-year mandate ends on Saturday 31 October. Russia vetoed a US draft that got 11 votes in favour, with 3 abstentions including China. The US draft would have extended the mission for a year, dropped "Referendum" from its name and made Morocco's 2007 autonomy plan the basis for talks. A Russian counter-draft for a plain one-year renewal then got only 3 votes, with the US voting against. MINURSO was set up in 1991 to monitor a ceasefire and organise a vote on independence or integration with Morocco, but the vote never took place. Morocco's royal palace called the outcome a "significant step" towards closing the file and said UN staff should leave. The Polisario Front (the Algeria-backed independence movement) welcomed the veto. US ambassador Mike Waltz said he was ready to work on an "orderly withdrawal", while France's delegate warned that an abrupt closure would be "exceedingly alarming" given renewed tensions.
why: the Council rarely lets a peacekeeping mission lapse this way. The ceasefire Polisario abandoned in 2020 loses its last international monitors, while low-level fighting continues.

headline: Poland's court standoff spills into street
summary: Clashes broke out at Poland's Constitutional Tribunal after a judge announced the suspension of its president, backed by the Tusk government and opposed by President Nawrocki.
display_body: Poland's fight over its Constitutional Tribunal turned into street clashes on Friday night, 30 October, after judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska announced the one-month suspension of tribunal president Bogdan Święczkowski and his deputy and claimed the presidency herself as the most senior judge. Justice minister and prosecutor general Waldemar Żurek said he had asked for both judges' immunity to be lifted, which would allow them to be prosecuted. Prime Minister Donald Tusk backed the move, calling the restoration of the rule of law "our duty". The tribunal's own X account called it a "coup d'état". Supporters of Law and Justice (PiS), the party that governed from 2015 to 2023 and appointed Święczkowski, protested outside. Police pushed back attempts to enter the building, and chairs and bottles were thrown at officers. President Karol Nawrocki cancelled a trip to Senegal and went into the court building early on Saturday with the Supreme Court's first president. The dispute began when Nawrocki refused to swear in judges elected by parliament and Święczkowski then barred them from the building.
why: Poland's government and president now dispute who legitimately runs the country's constitutional court, a year before parliamentary elections, and neither side has offered a compromise.

headline: Canada set to become EU associate member
summary: At a Montréal summit Canada and the EU launched an Alliance for the Future and said they are working towards making Canada the EU's first Associate Member.
display_body: Canada and the EU launched an "Alliance for the Future" at their summit in Montréal on Friday 30 October, and said they are working towards making Canada the EU's first "Associate Member", the closest possible tie short of joining. The leaders said the content and scope of that status will be worked out "over the coming months". They concluded a digital trade agreement and a competition-enforcement agreement. Canada joined the EU's supercomputing joint undertaking (EuroHPC), which gives its researchers access to the JUPITER machine, and opened talks to join Erasmus+ and the next Horizon Europe research programme. Canada also said it would take part in the EU's €90 billion loan to Ukraine and signed agreements on critical minerals. Prime Minister Mark Carney framed the deal as reducing dependence on the United States.
why: an "associate membership" for a non-European country would be a new form of tie to the EU. Switzerland has spent years negotiating a sector-by-sector package (Bilaterals III), so whatever Ottawa ends up getting will be a direct point of comparison.

headline: More tankers hit near Strait of Hormuz
summary: Tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz on 29 and 30 October; Oman evacuated 25 crew and Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed mine strikes.
display_body: More tankers were hit near the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday 29 and Friday 30 October. On Friday, Oman's navy evacuated the 25 crew of a Panama-flagged merchant ship that Oman's maritime security centre said "was targeted", setting it on fire. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Friday that two tankers using an "unauthorised route" had suffered "incidents" and been immobilised, and that a third, carrying two million barrels of oil, had "hit a naval mine". Iran's armed forces had said four tankers caught fire after hitting mines on Thursday, while the UK maritime agency UKMTO reported two attacks that day. The US Central Command (CENTCOM) recently said the main shipping lanes were clear of Iranian mines. The Iranian figures cannot be independently checked.
why: ships keep being hit in the main export route for Gulf oil despite US statements that the lanes are clear. That keeps fuel prices high, including in Switzerland, where the government is preparing for possible shortages.

headline: US clears 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine
summary: The US State Department approved a sale of 500 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine worth over $2 billion, pending Congress, paid by allies and EU loan funds.
display_body: The US State Department on Friday 30 October approved the sale of 500 Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine, worth more than $2 billion, according to its statement as reported by RTS. The sale still needs approval from the US Congress, and the statement gave no delivery schedule. Ukraine will pay with contributions from Canada, Germany and Norway and with money from the EU support loan, and "no US funds" are involved. Patriots are the only interceptors Ukraine has that can reliably shoot down Russia's most advanced missiles. President Volodymyr Zelensky said this week that Ukraine would receive on average 12 Patriot missiles a month in 2026, and last week he accused Washington of deliberately delaying them.
why: an approval is not a delivery. 500 missiles would be about three and a half years of supply at the rate Zelensky described, so the real test is when they arrive.

headline: COP17 closes with diluted biodiversity texts
summary: The COP17 biodiversity conference in Yerevan closed on 31 October with measures to implement the 2022 Global Biodiversity Framework, some watered down.
display_body: The UN biodiversity conference (COP17) in Yerevan, Armenia, closed on the morning of Saturday 31 October with agreement on measures to implement the 2022 Global Biodiversity Framework, the Swiss environment office said. Countries took stock of progress for the first time towards the 23 targets for 2030, including protecting at least 30% of land and sea ("30 by 30"). They agreed to look more closely at freshwater and mountain ecosystems over the next two years. Le Monde reports that about 50 texts were adopted after two weeks of talks, but that some decisions were watered down to reach consensus, with rich and poor countries split above all over who pays. RFI says states want to speed up cuts to public subsidies that harm nature.
why: the official statements describe a stocktake rather than new binding targets. The gap to "30 by 30" by 2030 is still open, and the fight over finance is unresolved.

headline: DR Congo Ebola deaths pass 5,000
summary: DR Congo authorities report 5,026 Ebola deaths since mid-May and more than 10,000 cases.
display_body: DR Congo's health authorities say 5,026 people have died of Ebola since mid-May, with more than 10,000 reported cases, NZZ reported on Saturday 31 October. That is up from just over 4,000 deaths at the start of October. 1,101 people are being treated or isolated and 2,788 have recovered. Experts think the virus spread unnoticed from at least February, before the outbreak was declared on 15 May, so the real toll may be higher. Africa CDC (the African Union's public-health agency) calls it the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record.
why: about a thousand deaths in four weeks shows the outbreak is still speeding up. Cases linked to travel have already appeared in Nigeria, and one patient was flown to Switzerland.

headline: RUAG probe finds serious failings
summary: A forensic probe found serious failings and signs of offences at RUAG; the DDPS froze possibly non-approved Leopard 2 spare parts and set up a working group.
display_body: The defence department (DDPS) said on Friday 30 October that a forensic investigation found "serious failings" and signs of criminal offences at the state-owned arms firm RUAG. As a precaution it has blocked all Leopard 2 tank spare parts in RUAG's stores that may have come from unapproved manufacturers. RUAG's board commissioned the law firm Niederer Kraft Frey to investigate in August 2023, after irregularities in the Leopard 1 tank affair. The report found that RUAG used material from consignment stocks (stock it held on behalf of the army) for business with third parties, and that parts made by unapproved producers from passed-on drawings may have ended up in RUAG's depots or in army tanks. Criminal proceedings are under way in Switzerland and Germany against former employees, who are presumed innocent. Defence minister Martin Pfister set up a working group that will report to the Federal Council within two to three months. The Council of States' security committee will debate the overhaul of the law governing federal arms companies no earlier than early 2027.
why: RUAG maintains much of the army's equipment, and the precautionary freeze affects the Leopard 2, the army's main battle tank. The federal audit office had already flagged problems with RUAG's stock management in a report published in January 2026.

headline: Hackers copy Vaud school user data
summary: An intruder copied names and school emails of about 3,500 teachers and 38,000 students from Vaud's post-compulsory schools' IT support platform.
display_body: The canton of Vaud said on Saturday 31 October that an intruder copied the names and school email addresses of about 3,500 teachers and 38,000 students at its gymnasiums and vocational schools, along with the content of their IT help requests. The unauthorised access to the schools' IT support platform was detected on Monday 26 October. The platform was taken offline and secured with help from the canton's security operations centre. No passwords were stored on it, and no grades or student files were affected. The canton has reported the incident to the Federal Office for Cybersecurity and the data-protection authority and will file a criminal complaint. RTS notes that it follows recent data thefts at an IT contractor of the federal pension fund Publica and at the Ricardo marketplace.
why: names plus school email addresses are exactly what targeted phishing needs. The canton is asking students and staff to treat urgent or unusual messages that seem to come from their school with suspicion.

headline: First Swiss Patriot parts due mid-2027
summary: Washington told the DDPS that Switzerland will receive a first Patriot fire unit by mid-2027 and may buy directly from the manufacturer, pending Congress.
display_body: Switzerland should receive the first parts of its delayed Patriot air-defence system by mid-2027, the US government told the DDPS on Thursday 29 October. The delivery will be one fire unit (a radar, a launcher and related equipment) taken from the original order and used for integration work and first training. The DDPS also got US agreement to buy the systems directly from the manufacturer instead of through the US government, subject to approval by the US Congress. Delivery slipped after Washington gave priority to Ukraine in July 2025, and the DDPS still expects full delivery to take five to seven years given the Middle East war.
why: a first unit in 2027 is for training, not operational air defence. The Federal Council has said it will not drop Patriot without a replacement, so Switzerland is left with a long-range air-defence gap for years.

headline: Lyon court refuses to halt A412 motorway
summary: The Lyon administrative court of appeal rejected Geneva's emergency request to suspend work on the A412 Machilly-Thonon motorway.
display_body: The administrative court of appeal in Lyon has rejected the City of Geneva's emergency request to halt work on the A412 Machilly–Thonon motorway in French Chablais, RTS reported on Friday 30 October, citing an order first revealed by Le Courrier. The court found that none of the arguments raised "serious doubt" about the legality of the French authorisation. The communes of Choulex, Presinge, Gy, Puplinge, Vandœuvres and Lancy had joined the request. Geneva's separate challenge to the environmental permit is still pending, so construction continues until the court rules on the merits. Geneva fears the road will bring more cross-border commuter traffic even though the Léman Express rail line serves the same corridor.
why: Geneva has little leverage over a French road that will feed traffic into the canton, and the fast-track route to stopping the work has now failed.
